findings.element: .b-behindSummary — the past disclosure, the only focusable element on every guest surface (phone, desk, day, print)
findings.problem: Driven at 320/390/1024/1440, rest and hover render byte-identical: same colour, background rgba(0,0,0,0), text-decoration none, no marker, no caret, no border. Only the cursor changes. At rest it is drawn in the same 11px mono uppercase fore-62 as DAYS AWAY, TODAY IS 16 JULY and KEPT BY ORLA, so it is typographically identical to the page's inert section labels. Opening it is equally undesigned: transition-duration is 0s and 138px (phone/desk) to 241px (day) of rows appear in a single frame with no animation. The one interaction the flagship guest is ever offered — a phone, once, judging the whole company — neither reads as pressable nor behaves like anything but a layout glitch when pressed. The gate proves the past can be asked for; nothing proves anyone could tell that it can.
findings.fix: Give .b-behindSummary a control treatment at rest and a real reveal. (1) Separate it from the micro-label family: keep the mono label but add a leading disclosure mark drawn from the existing tick vocabulary — a 7px hairline ring, border 1px solid var(--fore-46), filling to var(--fore) when open — and raise the summary's own colour to var(--fore) so it is denser than the fore-62 labels around it. (2) Add .b-behindSummary:hover { background: var(--fore-06); box-shadow: 0 0 0 8px var(--fore-06); border-radius: 4px; } — the same treatment .b-item:hover already gives .b-copy, so the two hover languages match. (3) Animate the reveal: give .b-behindDetails[open] .b-behindList an animation of var(--t-base) var(--ease) from translateY(-6px) and opacity 0, staggering each past row by 40ms, inside the existing prefers-reduced-motion block that already zeroes every transition.

findings.element: The Delete this moment control in the editor, and the .b-undoAct meant to reverse it
findings.problem: Measured on owner-editing with scrollY captured either side of the press: at 768 the page jumps 928px from the top of the document and 628px from scrollY 300; at 1024 it jumps 888px and 588px; at 1280 it jumps 527px from the top. The new position is already there at 120ms with scroll-behavior auto — an instant teleport of one to two screens, not a move. The owner is looking at the wedding-date hero, presses Delete in the sheet, and the surface is somewhere else with no motion connecting the two. Undo then restores the moment but not the place: the measured undo jump is 0px in every case, so pressing the way back leaves the owner exactly as lost. The cause is an unconditional scrollIntoView on the row that takes focus after the delete. This is the library's first lesson — repaints that annihilate place — creeping back, and it lives at 1024 and 320, two widths the behaviour gate never visits; its viewport list is 390, 768, 1280 and 1440.
findings.fix: In render-b.js, at the delete handler and every other whole-surface repaint, replace the unconditional scrollIntoView with a minimal one: capture window.scrollY and the focus target before the repaint, restore window.scrollY immediately after it in the same frame, then call target.scrollIntoView({ block: 'nearest' }) only when target.getBoundingClientRect() actually falls outside [0, window.innerHeight]. Store the captured scrollY on the history entry alongside the change, and have .b-undoAct restore that scrollY when it reverses the change, so the way back returns the view as well as the data. Add 320, 768 and 1024 to interaction-check.mjs's viewport list and assert that the absolute change in scrollY across delete, add and undo is at most 1px.

findings.element: Preview, Publish, and Back to the plan
findings.problem: Driven at 320/390/768/1024/1280/1440, all three rebuild the whole surface and leave document.activeElement as BODY with scrollY reset to 0. Nothing is announced: after Publish the .b-live region is empty and the arrived surface carries no h1. Three of the owner's five top-level actions are therefore silent screen changes for a keyboard or screen-reader user — press Publish and you are told nothing, and Copy the link, the entire point of that screen, sits two blind tab presses away. The return trip is the same: Back to the plan drops you at the document root and the row you were working on is seven tab stops down. The gate proves the way back exists and works; it never asks where the person went.
findings.fix: Route all three through one transition helper in render-b.js: once the new surface is built, move focus to its opening title (give each state's title tabindex="-1" and call focus({ preventScroll: true }) on it) and write one sentence into the existing .b-live role=status node — "The plan as guests will see it." for Preview, "Ready to send. The link is below." for Publish, "Back to the plan." for Back. On Back, additionally restore the scrollY and the id of the control that left the surface, refocusing that control when it still exists, so the round trip returns the owner to the row they were previewing.

findings.problem: Measured at 390: the loading frame draws four bars ending at y=200 in a document 844px tall. What arrives on phone is a count block at y=65..147 and a measure at y=348..1388 — a 1040px band the frame reserves 0px of. The promise is a small card and the delivery is a page twice the height, with everything below the fold arriving unannounced. The gate's assertion is that the loading frame invents no measure; that was satisfied by drawing nothing at all, which is the letter of the rule and the opposite of its intent — the library's rule is a reserve floor of one row, never two.
findings.fix: Add a measure band to the skeleton in render-b.js: after the four existing bars, emit the DAYS AWAY micro-label as real text (it is true before the data arrives), the vertical rule at its real x offset, and exactly one row skeleton — an away-number bar, a hollow tick and a title bar at the row's real 82px height and real left offset — then stop. Size the band to min(one row + 120px, remaining viewport) so the frame states that a measure is coming and where it starts, without promising a count of rows it does not yet know. Extend interaction-check.mjs to assert the loading frame's document height falls within 25% of the arrived phone surface's above-the-fold height.

findings.element: .b-grab / .b-grabWord in every measure row, against the Shown/Hidden pair inside the editor
findings.problem: The only visible control in a row is the word SHOWN. It is a status word, it sits where a status badge would sit, and pressing it opens a full editor. One screen away, inside that editor, the same word Shown is a real aria-pressed toggle that changes visibility. The identical string is a noun in the row and a verb in the panel, so the obvious guess — press SHOWN to make it hidden — is wrong in the first place a planner will try it. The row's hit area is the whole 520x83 block via .b-grab::after, which is right, and the row hover treatment is clean and reflow-free; but the 58x28 badge is the only part of the row that admits to being a control, and it advertises the wrong action.
findings.fix: Split the two jobs in render-b.js. Keep the whole-row ::after hit area and the accessible name ("Open Menu tasting at The Orchard..."), but change .b-grabWord's visible text from the visibility state to the action — "Edit" — and move the visibility state to a separate non-interactive mark: render "Hidden" as a static .b-hiddenMark on hidden rows only, in fore-62 alongside the existing dashed tick, and render nothing on shown rows, since shown is the default and does not need saying. Reserve the words Shown and Hidden for the editor's toggle alone, so each word means exactly one thing on the surface.

biggestWin: The stepper, ceiling and reversibility model on the owner surface is the best interaction work in the lab and would survive comparison with Linear. Driven 120 presses deep at 1440, scrollY held at 184 without a pixel of drift, focus never left the pressed button, and at the ceiling the control stayed enabled and said a true sentence — "This is as far as it goes. Wedding day is the last day." — instead of greying out and absorbing the press. The date readout is a role=status, so the new date is spoken on every step. Around it, one reversibility node travels between rail, editor and bottom edge, stays disabled and silent until something true has happened, names the change in plain words ("Send the invitations is now hidden from guests."), advertises Ctrl Z and honours it, and falls silent again when the stack empties. Every owner action — add, rename, type a date, step, hide, delete — is reversible by both the button and the key; refusals are specific and keep focus in the field; Escape returns focus to the row that opened the editor; and eleven states produced zero console errors.
